en: The Sūtra of the Samādhi Dhāraṇī of the Five Buddha-Uṣṇīṣas, Scroll One. Translated by the Tripitaka Master Bodhiruci of India during the Great Tang Dynasty, by Imperial Decree. Chapter One: The Introduction. **Chapter One: The Introduction** Thus have I heard. At one time the Bhagavat was dwelling in the palace of the King of the Nāgas, within the great jeweled pavilion of the Lotus Treasury Ocean, together with a great assembly of bhikṣus, twelve thousand in number; all were arhats, free from outflows, their minds liberated, their tasks accomplished, their lives sustained by their final bodies, having attained mastery over their own minds, like great elephants, with their defilements extinguished, having laid down their heavy burdens, reaching their own goal, with the fetters of existence completely severed, possessing right knowledge and right liberation, and being as great śrāvakas as there are in the world. Also present were bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, equal in number to the sands of the Ganges River, all of whom had already perfected the six pāramitās, possessed the ten powers, and were endowed with the four fearlessnesses. They were skilled in the profound gates of the Dharma, had attained the samādhis of the bodhisattvas, and were able to manifest the various transformations of the bodhisattvas. Their names were:

Thus have I heard.
At one time the Bhagavān was staying at the Great Jewel Treasury Canopy in the Vajra Seat beneath the Bodhi tree in the kingdom of Magadha, having newly attained perfect enlightenment.
Those jeweled canopies upon the ground were all produced through the supernatural powers, great merit, and virtuous deeds of the Tathāgata;
they were composed entirely of immeasurable, supreme, and wondrous rarities that manifested spontaneously and magnificently.
Various adornments of manifold colors reflect one another, emitting great radiance;
the extraordinary jewel-wheel is pure and perfect,
decorated with an intermingling of immeasurable hues.
It manifested, encircled on all sides,
with precious parasols, banners, and pennants shining with brilliant light;
exquisite fragrances, flower garlands, and nets of the seven treasures completely covered it from above.
The inexhaustible great jewels manifest with sovereign splendor;
these jewel trees have flowers and leaves that are lush and radiant.
Through the Buddha’s spiritual power, this site is made vast, magnificent, and pure.
Its radiance shines everywhere.
A multitude of all manner of extraordinary and wondrous jewels, accumulated from immeasurable roots of goodness, adorns the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*).
That Bodhi tree is lofty, prominent, and most exceptional.
Lapis lazuli forms its trunk, while exquisite jewel branches and precious leaves hang down like layered clouds;
various colored jewel flowers are interspersed with one another,
and great mani-jewels serve as its fruit.
Its light pervasively illumines all Buddha-fields,
manifesting various transformations to perform Buddha-works.

Through the spiritual power of the Bodhisattva Dharma of the One-Syllable Uṣṇīṣa-Cakra-Vartin King, it universally manifests the Mahāyāna teachings and produces various sublime Brahma-sounds to extol the immeasurable merits of the Tathāgata.
He was accompanied by countless great bodhisattvas,
such as the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Vajradhvaja and the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara.
Innumerable great bodhisattvas, all acting as leaders,
were gathered together with the entire great assembly beneath the wondrous Bodhi tree.
By the Buddha’s supernatural power, they sat in a circular assembly extending five hundred yojanas,
without obstructing one another. Therein,
the Tathāgata addressed Maitreya Bodhisattva and the other bodhisattvas, saying:
"O son of good family, this tree is the tree adorned by the Buddha's Bodhi.
When I first sat beneath this tree,
I shattered the four Māras and realized unsurpassed, perfect, and complete buddha-wisdom."
"You all should also sit upon this ground;
it shall cause you to attain the unsurpassed wisdom of a Buddha.
Having spoken these words, he became silent and motionless.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Vajrapāṇi,
by virtue of the Buddha’s majestic spiritual power and through the force of his own original vows made in the past, [proceeded].
He immediately rose from his seat, bared his right shoulder, adjusted his robes,
knelt with his right knee on the ground, joined his palms,
and gazing up at the Buddha with reverence, addressed him, saying:
"Bhagavān, I now inquire of the Tathāgata, the Perfectly Awakened One, regarding the *Cakravartin-śīrṣa-mantra* rite.
By what skillful means may one achieve sincere orientation toward all the *mahāvidyā-mantra* rites of the Tathāgatas with little effort?"
The ritual methods for the preparatory mandala and various mudrās;
the one-syllable Cakravartin rite;
the method for achieving accomplishment at the site of the Great Samādhi mandala; and the wheel of recitation and the method for binding mudrās.
The secret methods for painting images;
the methods for removing karmic obstructions; the methods for peace and security;
the methods for abundant wealth; and the methods for subduing māras and enemies.
The true Dharma of the lineage of all Tathāgatas;
the supreme vidyā-dharmas that are unimpeded in both the mundane and supramundane realms;
and the dharmas for accomplishing the conduct of Bodhisattvas throughout the entire realm of sentient beings.
This dhāraṇī rite shall cause all sentient beings within the realm of Jambudvīpa to attain great peace and happiness;
these sentient beings do so through the secret power of the Tathāgata as a Universal Monarch (cakravartin).
All shall perform great Buddha-activities, just as all sentient beings within this realm of Jambudvīpa attain great peace and happiness;
thus one will be able to accomplish this King of Uṣṇīṣa Dharma.
One will accordingly achieve success in all dhāraṇī-mantras of the devas and their lineages,
all dhāraṇī-mantras of the nāgas and their lineages,
and all dhāraṇī-mantras of the yakṣas and their lineages.
The incantation methods for all rākṣasas and all rākṣasa lineages;
the incantation methods for all gandharvas and their lineages;
the incantation methods for all asuras and their lineages.
The incantation methods for all garuḍas and all garuḍa lineages;
the incantation methods for all kinnaras and their lineages;
and the incantation methods for all mahoragas and their lineages.
Even unto all mundane and supramundane dharmas,
they achieve them all entirely without obstruction,
serving as a great dwelling place for all sentient beings.
It removes all defilements and obstacles, accomplishing my own mantra-dharmas,
as well as the altar, mudrā, and mantra-dharmas of Avalokiteśvara and the other great bodhisattvas of great majestic power,
and the immeasurable, difficult-to-accomplish altar, mudrā, and mantra-dharmas taught by all the Tathāgatas.
"Therefore, I pray that the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha,
out of compassion for sentient beings, will instruct me. At that time,
the World-Honored One addressed Vajrapāṇi, the Chief of Secret Traces, saying:
Excellent, excellent, you all!
You shall bring great benefit to all sentient beings of the future,
for you are able to inquire of me regarding this One-Syllable King, the Great Universal Monarch of the Crown.
It accomplishes all the secret maṇḍala rites and other methods taught by the Tathāgatas, causing all mantra-practitioners to abide in diligent cultivation.
Therefore, Guhyapāda, listen attentively, listen attentively; I shall now proclaim it.
All Tathāgatas of the past have already spoken it;
all Buddhas of the future shall likewise speak it.
At that time, the Tathāgata Śākyamuni—
He then surveyed all worlds and all sentient beings with the Buddha-eye,
as well as all worlds and all sentient beings of the future.
In each instance, at the places where roots of goodness had been planted through the power of past blessings and vows,
he addressed the bodhisattvas, saying:
"Sons of good family, you should all recollect the single-syllable Cakravartin mantra spoken by all the Tathāgatas."
This is the locus of all supreme samādhis and most inconceivable supernormal powers;
this Dharma is able to perform great Buddha-works in all worlds.
At that time, those bodhisattva-mahāsattvas received the Buddha’s instructions.
Each focused their minds upon the samādhi of the One-Syllable Cakravartin King, with the sole exception of the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara and the Bodhisattva Vajrapāṇi; why was this?
Because they were empowered by the Buddha.
Chapter Two: The Manifestation of Virtues through the Empowerment of Entering Samādhi. At that time, the World-Honored One entered the Great Samādhi of the Buddha’s Spiritual Transformation.
When entering samādhi,
having fully and universally brought to mind the entire realm of sentient beings,
one then [dedicates] the roots of virtue from the immeasurable six pāramitās accumulated and cultivated over immeasurable great kalpas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges.
From each of his thirty-two marks of a great man, he radiates a great light;
upon each mark, a Dharma-seal manifests,
and each is surrounded by various kinds of radiant light.
From the very summit of his head, he emitted and manifested immeasurable hundreds of thousands of rays of light;
these lights were of various colors and illuminated the ten directions.
Among them, sentient beings who encountered this light were each awakened and alerted by one another.
The light returned and circled the Buddha three times, each ray resuming its original form.
At that time, after Śākyamuni Tathāgata had emitted this light,
he slowly and calmly arose from his samādhi.
Beholding all the buddha-fields like a lion king,
and observing the assembled multitude, he addressed the Bodhisattva Vajrapāṇi, the Chief, saying:
"Listen now attentively to the Dharma of the King of Bright Mantras, the One-Syllable Uṣṇīṣa-Cakra-Rāja."
The four Uṣṇīṣa mantra-kings and the Buddha-eye Ūrṇā-kośa mantra-king—
these mantra-kings are the hands and feet of the Tathāgata.
These are the lips of the Tathāgata; these are the mouth of the Tathāgata.
As a Wheel-Turning Dharma King, he brings great benefit to all sentient beings.
Whether they be all the bodhisattvas in this world, or all other human beings, [he benefits them].
If one is able to recite, receive, and uphold this One-Syllable Wheel-Turning King’s Uṣṇīṣa-vidyā according to the Dharma,
then none of all the devas, worldlings, or various ghosts and spirits will be able to cause harm or create any destruction.
By this, one shall obtain all peace and happiness, receive immeasurable merit,
practice great compassion, and abide on the stage of non-retrogression;
one will be free from the afflictions of illness and the calamities of fire, water, weapons, kings, and the like.
Free from all poison, harm,
and the like, this single syllable of mine gives rise to the *samādhi* wheel-turning king mantra.
Should there be any newly initiated Mahāyāna bodhisattvas or other persons, [who recite it...]
Those who believe in, recite, uphold, transcribe,
or wear [this] shall be protected by immeasurable deities of great majesty and power.
No malevolent devas or nāgas shall obstruct or harass them, and they shall always enjoy peace and security.
If one is to transcribe it, they should first bathe thoroughly and don fresh, clean garments;
observing the precepts according to the Dharma,
they should sit beside the altar and write the mantra using realgar on birch bark.
It is to be bestowed upon bhikṣus and bhikṣuṇīs,
who shall tie it to the corner of their saṃghāṭī robes and wear it as an amulet.
If kings, members of royal families, ministers, officials, or sons and daughters of noble families wear it, [they shall likewise receive its protection].
If one wears it upon the head, fastens it around the neck, or binds it upon the wrists or arms,
one will attain peace and security, be freed from all calamities and afflictions,
and will always be beheld, honored, and praised by the devas.
It is for the purpose of ensuring that none fall into the various evil realms.
O Vajrapāṇi, this great King of Mantras can also extinguish all calamities caused by malevolent stars and portents, and bestow great peace and happiness.
It can also subdue all the devas, nāgas, and the eight classes of spirits;
it can also bring to fulfillment the various mantras of its respective section.
He then further addressed Vajrapāṇi, the Chief of Secret Traces:
This is the White Parasol Uṣṇīṣa King of all Tathāgatas,
the Mantra of the Transcendent Crown King, the Victorious Crown King, and the Radiant Mass Crown King;
it dwells equally within the samādhi of all Tathāgatas.
The supernatural powers [of these] are all equal, immeasurable, and vast;
yet they still cannot equal even a single syllable of the supreme samādhi mantra of the King of the Uṣṇīṣa.
Why is it supreme and peerless?
Just as with the Tathāgata-eye mantra and the Ūrṇā-kośa (hair-treasure) mantra,
or the mantras for the Tathāgata Maitreyajaya, the Buddha’s tooth, hand, alms-bowl, robe, and the turning of the wheel of Dharma—
only by reciting these mantras together does one attain the most supreme state.
Furthermore, from the roar of the Great Man of great compassion and great kindness,
which no great bodhisattvas or others can destroy,
all buddhas rejoice and bestow their empowerment.
Producing the light of great wisdom to shatter all darkness,
with firm and pure discernment capable of manifesting majestic power,
his auspicious marks of merit are the most supreme in the world.
Stainless, pure, courageous, and firm,
manifesting the four fearlessnesses and profound, virtuous wisdom,
he possesses vast, immeasurable, and supreme intelligence.
He is able to manifest the great radiant majesty of the ten powers of the adamantine uninterrupted [wisdom],
shattering all obscurations of darkness and entering the wisdom of all Buddhas;
he is able to accomplish all the merits of the myriad practices and all wisdom of the great Bodhisattvas.
It is the place of great majestic power, supremely unimpeded, courageous, tranquil, and capable of performing all [deeds];
it is the place where one can exercise great compassion toward all sentient beings who commit evil through their karma.
This is the samādhi place that can manifest the supernatural powers of all Tathāgatas.
Then he spoke this one-syllable vidyā-mantra of the Uṣṇīṣa King:
*Namaḥ samantabuddhānām oṃ bhrūṃ huṃ*. At that time, when the Tathāgata spoke this one-syllable Uṣṇīṣa-vidyā-mantra,
The trichiliocosm, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges,
shook in six ways all at once,
like the thickets and grasses of Jambudvīpa being blown by a fierce wind.
Within this, all the kings of mountains likewise shook violently;
all the sources of the oceans boiled over entirely;
and by the Buddha’s spiritual power, great fires broke out everywhere throughout all the palaces of the Māras.
Therein, all the māras, oppressed by the fire,
were utterly terrified and took refuge in the Buddha;
the sufferings of all hells were completely stilled.
At that time, the World-Honored One manifested the Great Majestic Power of the Single-Syllable Vidyā-Uṣṇīṣa-Cakravartin King.
Suddenly, he transformed his body into the form of a Great Cakravartin King,
fully manifesting the seven treasures and a complete retinue.
Within each and every jewel, a great circle of light is emitted, illuminating all infinite dharma-jewels; at once, various jewel-lights appear.
This Great Wheel-Turning King sits upon a precious throne.
His body was magnificent and radiant, emitting various kinds of light that illuminated everything like a mass of gold.
Among the sentient beings present in the assembly,
not a single being was able to look upon him.
This assembly consisted of all the great Bodhisattvas,
such as Maitreya and others, none of whom were able to gaze upon or behold [the Buddha].
There were also the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara and the Bodhisattva Vajrapāṇi.
By the Buddha’s majestic spiritual power, in an instant they became dazed and collapsed to the ground.
At that time, those gods of great majesty and virtue—
namely Maheśvara and Nārāyaṇa— [were likewise affected].
Śakra-devānām-indra, the deva Kuvēra, the deva Pāñcika,
the Māra-rāja Yama, and even all the various celestial deities,
as well as all the spirits and ghosts of great majestic power.
The wheels, halberds, pestles, nooses, clubs, and staves they grasped,
as well as all the weapons in the hands of their retinues, all fell away. At that time,
the Great Wheel-Turning King manifested the light of great compassion.
In order to cause all bodhisattvas to recollect the samādhi of the supernatural powers of awakening,
at that time, all the great nāgas, spirits, yakṣas, rākṣasas, gandharvas, and the other eight classes of beings [gathered].
At that time, struck with fear in the midst of battle, his body hairs stood on end;
none were able to gaze upon the countenance or the majestic radiance of the Great Wheel-Turning King.
Then, with a mind of equanimity, he took refuge in the Buddha, the World-Honored One, crying out: "Namo Buddhāya! Namo Buddhāya!"
At that time, for the sake of bringing about awakening and understanding in the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara, the Bodhisattva Vajrapāṇi,
and the great assembly, the World-Honored One quickly, in a mere moment,
concealed this majestic body and returned to his form as a Tathāgata.
I shall explain the Great Vidyā-mantra Mother, the Eye of All Buddhas.
This refers to those who are most fearsome and difficult to subdue;
it is for the purpose of accomplishing all worldly and supramundane vidyā-kings and wheel-turning kings.
In all matters and stages, it extinguishes all disputes and arguments.
This mantra is the mother-mantra of the lineage of all Buddhas;
it is further the mother who gives birth to and nurtures all the great Bodhisattvas, and it is also the mantra of the five eyes of all Buddhas.
Then he spoke the mantra, saying:
*Namaḥ sarvatathāgatebhyo viśvarūpābhyaḥ samyaksambuddhebhyaḥ oṃ ruru sphuru jvala tiṣṭha siddhalocane sarvārthasādhani svāhā*. Having spoken this mantra of the Eye of All Buddhas, he concluded.
When the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara and the Bodhisattva Vajrapāṇi had regained their senses,
they rose from the ground;
so too did all the celestial hosts endowed with majestic virtue.
Each attained their original mind, experiencing contentment and peace;
each grasped the weapon originally held in their own hand and,
with single-minded devotion, took refuge in the Buddha, gazing up at him and praising him, saying:
"How rare, World-Honored One! How rare, Sugata!
At that time, the two great beings joined their palms and addressed the Buddha, saying, "World-Honored One, Tathāgata, for what reason today..."
A great mass of light, specifically manifesting the marks of a wheel-turning monarch, appeared—most wonderful, rare, and never before seen.
The Tathāgata addressed him, saying: "O son of noble family!"
This is the Samādhi-gate of the Sovereign of the Uṣṇīṣa, which maintains the forms and miraculous transformations of all Buddhas;
it is, for example, like the various majestic powers manifested when you assemble in the great maṇḍala.
Regarding all such inconceivable miraculous manifestations and extraordinary events,
the Tathāgata likewise displays the marvelous physical color,
features, and majestic power of a great universal monarch (cakravartin).
This King of Summits is the body of the supreme samādhi in which all Tathāgatas abide;
no great bodhisattvas whatsoever are able to surpass it.
There is no king of mantras superior to this one.
In whatever place one recites this mantra,
for five yojanas around, it prevails both in the supramundane and the mundane realms.
All king-mantras are entirely without establishment or abiding.
If you speak of them in this same manner and location,
then the empowered great mantras will likewise have no establishment or abiding whatsoever.
If there is anyone who recollects this King of Pinnacles Dhāraṇī,
they shall attain the supramundane, and all mundane great dhāraṇīs will be completely accomplished.
As for all the dhāraṇīs of the various teachings you have spoken, if one recites and maintains them, they will prove ineffective.
If one constantly recites this mantra as an accompaniment to their chanting,
they will achieve success within five yojanas;
all bodhisattvas and vajra-mantra deities [will assist them].
The eight classes of devas and nāgas do not abide in, nor enter into, nor manifest the signs of accomplishment. Furthermore,
even the majestic power and spiritual might of all other supreme king-mantras cannot obtain a shadow,
let alone compare, with this Great Wheel-Turning King mantra.
Why is this? It is because the majestic power and spiritual efficacy of this mantra are most honored, extraordinary, and peerless.
Even the bodhisattvas of the ten stages are terrified by the majestic virtue and supernatural power of this mantra.
How much more so for the gods!
Whenever one recites this mantra of the Wheel-Turning King,
one must first recite the Buddha-Eye mantra seven times.
Once the counting is complete, one should then recite this Cakravartin King mantra.
When the counting is finished, one should further recite the Buddhalocanā mantra seven times;
thus, one will attain peace and security, free from all disturbances and afflictions.
At that time, the World-Honored One again manifested upon his seat the body of the King of Mantras,
the White Parasol Uṣṇīṣa, empowered by all Buddhas;
at which moment, it appeared directly above his head.
A single canopy appeared, extending across the entire expanse of space throughout the trichiliocosm,
yet it did not disturb or harm the sentient beings dwelling in the sky.
At that time, the two bodhisattvas Avalokiteśvara and Vajramukha—
Joining his palms, he addressed the World-Honored One, saying:
"World-Honored One, what are the causes and conditions for such a miraculous transformation?
Suddenly, the great trichiliocosm is pervaded, appearing like a parasol."
It abides above the crown of the Buddha’s head, its limits unseen and its meaning entirely understood.
The World-Honored One declared:
"This is the White Parasol Crown King, spoken by immeasurable Tathāgatas in concert."
Furthermore, there are the infinite jewel-precious forms and infinite sounds of all Tathāgatas;

This is the mantra of the Great Vidyārāja,
which the Tathāgata now speaks for the sake of all sentient beings attaining great peace and happiness.
If the practitioner encounters a person of violent and wicked character,
he should rub his face with his hand while silently reciting this mantra,
and then engage that person in discourse on the principles of the Dharma.
One shall obtain that joy and gladness,
and will also be able to subdue all *chima*, *manglang*, and malevolent spirits. Lord Guhyapati,
if a person upholds this Cakravartin-king mantra, [they shall attain these benefits].
If the dharma one prays for and the dharma for which one seeks realization are not accomplished,
then one should add this Great Vidyā-rāja and recite both equally for a full two hundred thousand times.
If one recites the mantra of the Supreme Siddhi of the King of Uṣṇīṣas with the certainty of accomplishment without first performing these one or two ritual procedures,
it will cause harm and misfortune to the body of the mantra-holder.
Next is the Eighteenth: the Tathāgata’s Brow-Mudrā Mantra. This is identical to the Tathāgata’s Eye-Mudrā, with the sole modification being that the two index fingers are changed.
Place each [finger] on the back joint of the middle finger,
with the tip separated from the middle finger joint by about one *aṅgula*.
The mudrā and mantra are as follows:
*Namo samantabuddhānāṃ hṛ huṃ.* This is the mantra of the ūrṇā-kośa (hair-treasure) seal between the eyebrows of all Tathāgatas,
which has been proclaimed by all Tathāgatas.
I shall now also explain this:
when this mudrā is turned,
Maheśvara, Kumāra, Mahākāla, and the other deities shall not cause any affliction or disturbance.
How much less could minor goblins, demons, or spirits cause any affliction?
Next is the Nineteenth Mantra of the Tathāgata’s Mouth-Seal; this Nineteenth Mantra of the Tathāgata’s Mouth-Seal is to be understood according to the Tathāgata’s Heart-Seal.
Only change the two thumbs:
extend them along the shoulder blades and bend the tips of the joints equally.
At a distance of two barley grains from the side of the right index finger,
place the seal at the face-gate (mukha-dvāra).
These are the back joints of the heads of the two thumbs.
Place it precisely between the lips.
The seal-mantra is:
*Namaḥ samantabuddhānāṃ jiri jiri hūṃ*. This single seal-mantra possesses a great flaming torch.
This can swiftly assist in accomplishing all undertakings.
If the practitioner constantly forms this seal and places it between their lips while reciting this oral mantra two,
three, or twenty-one times:
Furthermore, for one who recites the Cakravartin King Mantra,
by the power of the mudrā and the mantra,
the gods and humans of the three realms shall see, hear, and engage in discourse with them.
All will respect and love them.
Therefore, this person should always speak with words that are harmonious, refined, true, and gentle.
Such a person shall not suffer from ailments of the mouth for hundreds of thousands of koṭis of kalpas.
When Maheśvara, Viṣṇu, and all the devas,
nāgas, and the eight classes of spirits heard these words of this person,
they were all humbled and submitted in reverence.
How much more so for other minor goblins, demons, and spirits.
Regarding the twenty seals and mantras of the Invincible Wrathful King (Durjayaparākrama-rāja), one should place the right knee upon the ground.
The left leg is bent with the knee pressed to the ground.
He assumes a posture as if about to rise and step forward, with his body leaning back, his face turned upward, his eyes staring intensely,
and his gaze cast askance toward the left side.
One should position the right arm, fingers, and so forth,
with the right side facing backward,
holding the arm askew and taut.
The arms are extended as if toward the ground;
the five fingers are splayed wide apart,
and the palms appear either turned downward or tilted sideways.
Next, turn the left arm to the left side and behind the body;
raise it with urgency and force, bending the arm and hand upward,
with the five fingers slightly spread.
Extend the thumbs upward and spread them apart,
with the palms facing forward.
When forming this mudrā:
If one utters a great roar of anger,
reciting the syllables "Hūṃ" twenty-one times,
all obstructing sins will be destroyed accordingly.
The Māra King of the desire realm and all his military generals have been utterly crushed.
In the past, when I first went to the Nairañjanā River to bathe my body, I proceeded to this foot of the Bodhi tree.
Seated upon the Vajra Throne,
at that time there shall be immeasurable hundreds of thousands of koṭis of māras,
each assuming various foul, impure, and wrathful forms.
When he was tormenting me,
Duṣprasaha became enraged and suddenly leaped up from the ground before me,
manifesting the form and appearance of a woman.
Sealing this with the seal of the destruction of hatred, all hosts of māras are crushed;
various terrifying forms are simultaneously dispersed and extinguished,
such that none are able to cause affliction.
During that night, as the dawn was about to break,
he realized the unsurpassed perfect knowledge of direct penetration;
he observed that among all the śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas in the world, there was no one who had realized it.
The mantra for the Seal of Subduing Māras is as follows:
Namo samantabuddhānām | Oṃ huru huru caṇḍini ṭaṅki svāhā | Vajrapāṇi.
This is the mantra of the Wrathful King Durjaya,
which I have spoken.
If a practitioner of this mantra should encounter places of great evil, fear, malevolent spirits, and the like, [it shall protect them].
One who wishes to protect their person by establishing a boundary (*sīmābandha*) and perform the ritual of accomplishment should apply themselves with diligent vigor;
they should bind this mudrā and recite this mantra.
If one practices this dharma with dedication, there will be no obstacles or afflictions, for it is swiftly accomplished.
Next, regarding the twenty-first mantra of the Tathāgata-śakti-mudrā: straighten the body and sit in the full lotus posture (paryaṅka).
With the left arm, turn the palm upward;
bend and extend it horizontally so that it is positioned directly below the navel,
with the four fingers joined and extended straight.
Slightly bend the right thumb and extend it straight,
pressing its tip against the side of the base of the index finger;
then, with the left hand, join the tips of the thumb and index finger together.
The middle, ring, and little fingers are joined together,
all slightly extended as if slightly bent.
The tips of the thumb and index finger are pressed against the tip of the little finger of the right hand.
This is the Seal of the Single Dharma.
The wise who constantly turn, maintain,
and bind it will manifest in this life and be born in future lives.
Never regressing in the power of faith, diligence, and wisdom, and through the power of the Tathāgata’s practice,
one obtains the protective mindfulness of all Tathāgatas.
The seal-mantra is as follows:
Namo samantabuddhānām. Oṃ mīrajaye mahāśodhi buddharakṣa hūṃ phaṭ | mīraye ni phaṭ | māgale phaṭ | svāhā. This is the dhāraṇī-mantra.
Recite this three times each day for twenty-one days;
one will swiftly attain unimpeded mastery throughout the three realms due to this supreme accomplishment.

Next is the twenty-second, the Tathāgata Navel Seal Mantra. It is identical to the Tathāgata Spear Seal, with the sole modification being that the tips of the right hand’s thumb and index finger are changed.
Moving away from the tip of the left little finger by the distance of one grain of barley is this Dharma-mudrā,
also known as the Great Powerful Hero Mudrā of all Buddhas.
If a wise person constantly maintains the wheel-seal and recites the navel-mantra,
they will be able to eliminate fevers lasting one or two days,
jaundice, intestinal headaches, and all such diseases.
Furthermore, all calamities and obstacles will naturally be extinguished.
One's lifespan, merit, and life-force shall become secure, peaceful, and prosperous.
The mantra and mudrā are as follows:
*Namo samantabuddhānām. Oṃ cici cici svāhā.* This is a dhāraṇī-mantra that can manifest the Tathāgata’s various forms and inconceivable supernatural transformations.
To entice sentient beings:
next, one should perform the Tathāgata-kavaca-mudrā twenty-three times; for this, one should use the right thumb.
Lay the hands flat across the palms.
With the index, middle, ring, and little fingers,
firmly grasp the thumbs to form fists.
This single Dharma-seal is named the Heart-Seal of the Sovereign King of All Summits.
If a wise person constantly seals their crown, neck, left and right shoulders,
and heart with this seal, they shall attain great majestic power.
The mantra-practitioner must diligently uphold and cultivate the Dharma;
without these seals, there is no adornment,
just as a form is naked and ugly.
It is like a country without a ruler, a house without an inhabitant,
food without salt, a pond that has dried up,
or the earth empty and devoid of groves, flowers, and grasses.
It is like a non-Buddhist Brahmin who worships fire and has no dharma to rely upon;
it is like a king riding in a chariot without a driver to control it.
Although the mantra-practitioner may thus apply themselves with diligent effort,
if they lack the armoring seal (*kavaca-mudrā*), they will be harassed by Māra and achieve no efficacy.
The mantra for the seal is as follows:
Namo samantabuddhānām | Oṃ krodharāja hūṃ | This dharma-mantra is named the Tathāgata-vajrapada-samādhi.
Just as a king who constantly protects himself by donning armor and strictly equipping himself with weapons has no fear of the hosts of evil thieves and soldiers,
so too is it with this mantra.

If one diligently practices this *nakha-mudrā* (nail-seal) three times daily, measuring one's strength and according to the ritual rules, one will swiftly achieve accomplishment because there is nothing to fear.
Next is the twenty-fourth, the *tathāgata-śikhā-mudrā-mantra*. This is the same as the preceding *nakha-mudrā*, with the sole modification that the middle fingers are extended and held upright.
Place the seal upon the crown of the head with the fingers held straight up and erect.
The mantra is:
*Namaḥ samantabuddhānām āḥ*. This seal and mantra are called the Tathāgata-keśa-samādhi-mukha (The Gate of the Tathāgata’s Hair Samādhi).
Its power is able to accomplish all undertakings.
Next is the twenty-fifth, the Tathāgata Ear Seal Mantra; it is performed according to the previous Nail Seal.
Simply change the position of the index fingers by extending them straight upward.
Place the mudrā vertically at the openings of the ears, level with the upper cartilage of the ears. The mantra for this mudrā is as follows:
*Namo samantabuddhānāṃ hūṃ ka*. This seal and mantra are named the Tathāgata-ear Samādhi-gate.
One should constantly form this seal and recite this mantra over the ears.
One shall swiftly eliminate all ailments of the ear and realize the supernormal power of the divine ear (*divya-śrotra-abhijñā*).
Next is the twenty-sixth mantra of the Tathāgata’s Tooth Seal (*tathāgata-danta-mudrā*): First, with the left hand, [use] the index, middle, ring, and little fingers.
Quickly bend [the arm] and clench the fist so that the shoulder blade is not exposed.
Then, extend the thumb straight upward and press it against the side of the head above the index finger.
The first line on the surface of the thumb is level with the outer back of the index finger;
place the seal upon the left jaw.
The right [hand] is likewise.
The mudrā and mantra are as follows:
*Namaḥ samantabuddhānāṃ oṃ tathāgatadaṃṣṭre huṃ phaṭ svāhā*. This single mudrā and mantra is named the Tathāgata-Teeth-Mudrā Samādhi-gate.
Possessing great majestic power,
one should recite this mantra and form the mudrā to seal the teeth;
thereby, in a future age, one shall obtain the Buddha’s teeth.

The Twenty-Seventh: The Seal and Mantra of the Tathāgata’s Prophecy. Regarding the Twenty-Seventh: The Seal and Mantra of the Tathāgata’s Prophecy: Hold the right arm straight and level across the chest;
then, with the index, middle, ring, and little fingers, form a tight fist.
The thumb is held upright and bent,
its tip positioned two finger-widths from the side of the index finger;
this is the dhāraṇī-mantra of all Tathāgatas of the past.
All Tathāgatas of the future and all Tathāgatas of the present receive their predictions of enlightenment by means of this seal.
Therefore, the wise should constantly form this seal to bestow the prophecy of bodhisattvahood upon all sentient beings.
The mantra of the seal is as follows:
*Namo samantabuddhānām oṃ hūṃ ṭraḥ*. This seal-mantra is able to accomplish all the activities of the Tathāgatas.
By the power of this seal and mantra,
in every successive birth one shall always obtain the power of mindfulness, the power of diligence, the firm power of precepts and meditative concentration,
and the superior power of the aggregates of merit; thus, one shall not be afflicted or disturbed by any evil ghosts or spirits.
Next is the twenty-eighth, the Tathāgata-shoulder-seal mantra. It follows the previous nail-seal, with the only difference being that the arms are extended straight upward.
The mudrā and mantra are as follows:
Namaḥ samantabuddhānāṃ, bhañja āsi phaṭ svāhā. This mudrā and mantra are named the Tathāgata-shoulder-mudrā samādhi-gate.
Because it possesses great supernormal power, is exceptionally courageous, and accomplishes all dharmas.
Next is the twenty-ninth, the Tathāgata-stana-mudrā mantra; this twenty-ninth Tathāgata-stana-mudrā mantra follows the previous nail-seal (nakhāṅgulī-mudrā).
Only change the position by bending the arm so that the fist seals the face.
Place the seal upon the heart.
The mantra for the seal is as follows:
Namo samantabuddhānām. Hūṃ bhaḥ. This one-seal mantra is named the Tathāgata-stana-mudrā-samādhi-dvāra.
Next, regarding the thirty-second mantra of the Tathāgata-dhvaja-mudrā:
first, with the right hand, place the thumb across the backs of the middle, ring, and little fingers.
Extend the index finger straight upward and hold it erect;
extend the arm directly above.
The mudrā and mantra are as follows:
Namo samantabuddhānām. *Kṣa* (the syllable *kṣa* is not pronounced). This is the name of a single-seal mantra, the Samādhi-gate known as the Tathāgata-Dhvaja-mudrā.
Next, the thirty-first: the Tathāgata Bedding Seal Mantra. Following the previous Banner Seal, turn the hands so that the index fingers point downward toward the chest.
The mudrā and mantra are as follows:
Namo samantabuddhānām āḥ guluk. This mudrā and mantra are named the Tathāgata-śayanāsana-mudrā-samādhi-dvāra (the Gate of the Samādhi of the Tathāgata’s Reclining Utensils).

Next, the thirty-second Tathāgata-yāna mudrā and mantra: following the previous banner mudrā, change the arm by bending it so that the hand is placed at the side of the heart, while the forearm is extended straight out.
The mudrā and mantra are as follows:
*Namaḥ samantabuddhānāṃ hūṃ kābuṃ oṃ*. This mudrā and mantra is named the Tathāgata-yāna-mudrā-samādhi-dvāra.
Next, the thirty-third: the Tathāgata Head Seal Mantra. Following the previous Banner Seal, change it so that the sealing hand is placed upon the crown of the head.
The mudrā and mantra are as follows:
Namaḥ samantabuddhānām, oṃ murdhne svāhā. This single mudrā and mantra is named the Tathāgata-Mūrdha-Mudrā Samādhi-gate.
Next, the thirty-fourth mantra of the Tathāgata’s Side-Seal (Pārśvamudrā): With the right hand, double-bend the heads of the ring finger and little finger.
Rest the back of the thumb against the palm;
extend the index and middle fingers side by side, straight and upright.
The mantra for this mudrā is as follows:
*Namo samantabuddhānām oṃ hūṃ khaḥ*. This one-seal mantra is called the Tathāgata-Parśva-mudrā Samādhi-dvāra.
Next is the thirty-fifth Tathāgata-Darśana-mudrā mantra: bend the tip of the middle finger of the right hand.
It is pressed against the tip of the right thumb;
the index, ring, and little fingers are aligned together,
extended straight upward, and held erect.
The mudrā and mantra are as follows:
Namo samantabuddhānām. Oṃ pāra-siddhi-kari svāhā. This is the single mudrā and mantra.
This is called the Tathāgata’s Samādhi Door of Perceiving the Nature of All Dharmas.
Next is the thirty-sixth [mantra] of the Tathāgata’s Light-Flame Seal; this thirty-sixth mantra of the Tathāgata’s Light-Flame Seal follows the previous "Perceiving Seal."
Only change the head-fingers— the ring finger and the little finger—
so that they face the palm, spread apart, and are slightly bent like the crescent of the new moon.
The mudrā-mantra is as follows:
*Namo samantabuddhānām oṃ jvalani svāhā*. This single-seal mantra is named "The Tathāgata’s Illumination of All Dharmas.
Next is the thirty-seventh: the Tathāgata’s Illumination Seal-Mantra. With the right hand, using the thumb...
Extend the thumb upward and press it against the side of the head-finger;
keep the head-finger straight and erect,
and extend the middle and ring fingers.
Each [finger] is extended toward the palm;
they are bent like the crescent moon,
and the ring fingers are also directed toward the palms.
Bend it into the shape of a hook.
The seal-mantra is:
*Namaḥ samantabuddhānāṃ oṃ hūṃ maṃ phaṭ svāhā*. This single seal and mantra is named "The Tathāgata’s Illumination of All Samādhi Gates."
Because it manifests in perfection.
Next is the Tathāgata Lip Seal Mantra (38). The Tathāgata Lip Seal Mantra (38) follows the previous Radiant Light Seal.
Only modify the middle finger by slightly extending it firmly between the grains of barley.
The mudrā and mantra are as follows:
*Namo samantabuddhānām āḥ vaṃ haṃ*. This one-syllable mantra is named the Tathāgata-oṣṭha-samādhi.
By holding it, one shall attain the extinction of all transgressions.
Next, the thirty-ninth: the Tathāgata Tongue Seal Mantra. With the right hand, using the index, middle, ring, and little fingers...
Place both hands together against the chest,
with the palms facing upward and extended flat;
the thumbs should lie across the center of the palms.
The mudrā and mantra are as above for the homage.
Oṃ nārani dhañja sūryacandrarāja hūṃ phaṭ svāhā. This single mudrā and mantra is named the Tathāgata-jihvā-samādhi (Tathāgata’s Tongue Samādhi).
The holder shall obtain the merit of the Tathāgata’s tongue-mark being perfected.
Next, regarding the forty [recitations] of the Tathāgata-samādhi-mudrā-mantra: with the five fingers of the left hand joined together.
Place the palms flat and extended sideways at a distance of two barley grains below the navel; then,
join the four fingers of the right hand together.
Likewise, with the hands tilted sideways, the palms are turned upward and extended flat;
the backs of the hands press down upon the left palm,
while the right thumb is bent across and tucked into the palm.
The mudrā and mantra are as above:
*Namaḥ* [as before], *oṃ adhiśayavikrami svāhā*. This single mudrā and mantra is named the Tathāgata-nābhi-samādhi.
Next, the forty-first Tathāgata-vajrajvālāmudrā-mantra; the forty-first [mantra] of the Tathāgata-vajrajvālāmudrā is the same as the preceding samādhi.
Change it to the heart-mantra.
The seal and mantra are as follows: *Namo* (as above).
*Hūṃ hūṃ jvala vajra kiṃkara kiṃkara guhyakādhipate*. This is the seal and mantra of the Vajra Flame of this [deity].
It is also called the King of Great Mantra-Spells of the Samādhi of the Vajra-Flame Heart of all Tathāgatas of the past, future, and present,
as well as for all Mahāsattvas who have realized the stages.

Furthermore, among the devas, nāgas, the eight classes of spirits, and those of great majesty and virtue, none are able to transgress [this seal], let alone other inferior beings such as *chi-mei* demons and ghosts.
Next is the forty-second mantra of the Tathāgata’s Lower Abdomen Seal: with the right hand, one places it one inch below the navel.
Extend the arms horizontally with the palms facing upward and the five fingers joined together.
Next, extend the five fingers of the left hand and place them back-to-back,
pressing down upon the palm of the right hand.
Place both hands on the side of the abdomen.
The mudrā and mantra are as follows: *Namo* (as above).
*Oṃ tsaṭ tsaṭ sa sa bhuvaṃ bhuvaṃ mṛdane pramardane cūrṇane bhindane hūṃ phaṭ svāhā*. The efficacy of this mudrā and mantra is the same as described previously.
Next, regarding the forty-third mantra of the Tathāgata’s Spinal Seal:
with the right hand, press the thumb against the tips of the index, ring, and little fingers.
Do not allow the fingernails to be exposed.
Next, cross the middle finger over the top of the thumb.
The mudrā and mantra are as follows: "I take refuge as before."
*Īṃ vīkāriṇa kāraṅgadhajaturonāramani nara svāhā.* The efficacy of this single-seal mantra is the same as described previously.
Next is the forty-fourth, the Tathāgata Thigh Seal Mantra. It is performed according to the previous Spine Seal;
however, one changes the position by pressing the nail of the middle finger’s head and extending the head of the index finger to press upon the nail of the thumb.
The mudrā and mantra are as follows:
Homage as before. Oṃ dhuta dhara svāhā. The efficacy of this single dharma-mudrā is according to the previous [description].
Next is the forty-fifth: the Tathāgata’s Great Compassion Mudrā and Mantra. This is according to the previous spine mudrā.
Again, shift the pressure to the tip of the index finger and the base of the little finger;
extend the tip of the ring finger and press it upon the base of the thumb.
For the sake of all sentient beings burdened by heavy defilements,
I have taught and revealed the Seal of Loving-kindness (maitrīmudrā) to cause them to give rise to a compassionate mind.
In the past, I sat beneath the Bodhi tree.
By binding this seal with a mind of great compassion,
all demonic armies will naturally disperse and submit.
Whoever binds this seal—
By means of the power of all Buddhas, the power of the Dharma, the power of Arhats, and the power of the mind of compassionate mindfulness, one should maintain this seal;
thus, all extremely heavy karmic stains and defilements will be swiftly and completely extinguished.

The mantra is: *Namo bhagavate tadyathā | kuṇḍalini | aṅkuravi-māla-pratyaṅga-sarva-ra-kṣa rakṣa mā hūṃ kumari śrīyamālini svāhā*. This single-seal mantra is named "The Great Compassion Seal Mantra of All Tathāgatas."
If there is a mantra-practitioner who constantly gives rise to a mind of loving-kindness and maintains this mantra-seal,
they shall not be harmed by any vināyakas.
Tigers, wolves, resentful enemies, strife, calamities, and sudden afflictions shall be pacified.

Because one swiftly realizes the *samādhi* of a compassionate mind through the power of this seal and mantra, next follows the Forty-Sixth Tathāgata Vimalamudrā Mantra; this is identical to the preceding Seal of Compassion.
Furthermore, change the tip of the ring finger and press it beneath the thumb;
next, press the tip of the little finger upon the nail of the thumb.
The mudrā and mantra are as follows:
Namaḥ samantabuddhānāṃ, huṃ mūrdhadhāriṇe hulu hulu huṃ phaṭ svāhā. This is the mudrā and mantra.
The wise person constantly recites mantras over their food and drink;
by consuming and partaking of it, they can extinguish all sins.
Furthermore, they will never be afflicted or harmed in their food by the Vināyakas.
Next, regarding the forty-seventh mantra of the Tathāgata Amṛta-mudrā: again, with the right thumb.
Cross the thumb, middle finger, ring finger, little finger, and the *kaniṣṭhikā* (pinky) [over the palm].
The seal-mantra is as follows:
*Namaḥ samantabuddhānāṃ oṃ indriya-indra-hīna svāhā*. This seal-mantra enables the practitioner to realize the Dharma of Ambrosia (*amṛta*) and the Great Gate of Liberation (*mahā-vimokṣa-mukha*).
Next, regarding the forty-eighth mantra of the Tathāgata’s Great Lion’s Roar Seal: first, join the palms at the heart.
The thumbs of both the left and right hands are each bent within the palms; furthermore,
the two index fingers, two middle fingers, two ring fingers, and two little fingers of each hand [are likewise positioned].
Bend and grasp the thumb to form a fist;
as for the left and right index fingers, middle fingers, ring fingers, and little fingers,
each should have its back turned inward and joined together.
The tips of these eight fingers must not touch the palms.
The mudrā and mantra are as follows:
*Namo samantabuddhānām. Oṃ kapi-la-re-ṭi-la huṃ phaṭ svāhā.* This single mudrā and mantra is named "The Great Lion’s Roar," the Vajraśekhara-samādhi-rāja-tantra for Accomplishment.
Because it is able to extensively manifest all inconceivable and unprecedented matters that transcend the mind;
next, the forty-nine times of the Tathāgata-lakṣaṇākṣara-mudrā-mantra, and furthermore, using the eight fingers of both the left and right hands.
Each finger is extended and spread apart;
the right hand presses down upon the left, with the fingers interlaced and pressing against each other at the middle joints.
The tips of all eight fingers are held straight and upright, extended without touching the spaces between them.
The two thumbs are likewise each extended diagonally upward;
extending the tips so they are one and a half inches apart,
place the seal at a distance of three inches from the chest.
The mudrā and mantra are as follows:
Namaḥ samantabuddhānāṃ. This mudrā and mantra, consisting of two syllables, is named the Tathāgata-mahāpuruṣa-lakṣaṇa-mudrā-samādhi-dvāra.
Next, for the fifty [recitations] of the Tathāgatalocanā-śrī-mudrā-mantra: join the left and right wrists together so that they touch.
Her ten fingers were spread apart and held upright;
with her head slightly bent and extended,
each finger was separated by an interval of one and a half inches, like an opening lotus flower.
The mudrā and mantra are as follows:
*Namaḥ samantabuddhānām oṃ sumbarakamale kṣami svāhā*. This mudrā and mantra are named the Tathāgata-Śrī-mudrā-samādhi.
It enables the holder to obtain great wealth and treasures and to be honored and praised by all people.
Next is the fifty-first *mudrā* and mantra of the Tathāgata’s Prajñāpāramitā: join the two hands into fists with the palms hollowed out.
Like an unopened lotus bud.
The mantra for the seal is: *Namo yathā pūrvavat*.
